# Broadcast source filtering experiment notes

The investigation keeps two names separate: broadcast source filtering and Redisson empty keys in batch operations. Both appear in the validation materials for the R2026.09 compatibility window, but there is no evidence yet that they share an implementation path. This page keeps the filtering experiment itself; empty keys in batch operations remain a parallel investigation item. Nothing without logs is recorded as a result.

## Where to start

The earlier investigation traced the issue name and call name to `jetcache-core/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/support/CacheMessage.java`. The header of `v_prev` directly shows:

```java
package com.alicp.jetcache.support;
import java.io.Serializable;
```

What is confirmed is the declaration location and navigation relationship for this file. The file path is not a substitute for the actual call context, nor does it establish where the broadcast manager, consumer or Redisson adapter belongs. Start the next rerun from this path as well: first locate where the message object is created, read and passed to broadcast handling, then record the actual parameters.

## Procedure notes

Change only the source value in each filtering experiment; keep all other inputs unchanged. Record three things: the source ID carried by the message, the source ID of the active broadcaster, and the state of the local cached value after processing. If a routing change is also observed, record it separately. Do not equate “the message was ignored” with “routing changed.” Do not mark success or failure unless the original parameter order and return status have been saved.

The finding after this round of review is: broadcast handling compares the source ID of CacheMessage. Messages with the same source ID as the active broadcaster preserve the local value; messages from other sources trigger invalidation, without changing operation routing.

This finding applies only to this version. The earlier investigation's claim that “a different source is skipped” was too broad and can no longer be used to explain whether the local value is preserved. The available material still does not establish whether the comparison occurs on the sending side, the receiving side or a wrapper layer between them. Check the neighboring source code; do not assign it a class name in advance.

## Empty keys in batch operations

No command output is recorded here yet. Without help text, an argument string or Redisson runtime logs, we cannot determine whether an empty key is rejected as input, transformed, or left as an empty entry in the batch operation. On the next run, add only the actual input and return status for this item; do not change the source filtering condition at the same time. If raw output is still unavailable, leave the status unconfirmed.

# Batch Cache and Notification Decision Record

This record originally placed batch null caching and the notification consumer lifecycle in the same compatibility window. The shared window still has value: both items left points requiring verification in the regression materials, and neither can be closed out based on a single superficial observation. However, the window is an arrangement, not a description of the mechanism.

The initial working assumption was a convenient one: after tracing how null is handled along the cache entry point, the differences in the notification-side situation might become easier to explain. That assumption was not retained after review. The two lines can appear in the same round, but there is no material showing that either one caused the other. The current decision is not to look for a single common cause, but to split the conclusions that can be recorded back across their respective objects.

`LoadingCache` is the starting point for the batch line, not proof of ownership of the notification lifecycle. The frozen path is `jetcache-core/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/LoadingCache.java`, the file is under the `com.alicp.jetcache` package, and the header directly shows `CacheEvent`, `HashMap`, and `LinkedHashSet`. These names are enough to indicate that the review should look at how keys are retained in batch requests, how results are collected, and whether event adjacency is actually used at the call site; they cannot by themselves determine the storage semantics of null.

Three ways of writing this were considered at the time.

| Handling | Problem | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treat the two items as the same compatibility defect | This would turn an unconfirmed causal relationship into a conclusion | Do not adopt |
| Look at `LoadingCache` first, then also assess the consumer state | The cache file can provide a local entry point, but cannot replace the notification-side evidence | Do not adopt |
| Record them separately while retaining the shared regression window | The release context remains, and the two judgments will not overwrite each other | Adopt |

This choice has one direct consequence: regression records cannot contain only “window passed” or “window failed.” The batch path and notification path must record their observations separately. If one line does not yet have an input or result, the other line’s record cannot be filled in under its name.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Compatibility Window
    Compatibility Window --> Batch_null_Cache
    Compatibility Window --> Notification_consumer_Lifecycle
    Batch_null_Cache --> LoadingCache_Review
    Notification_consumer_Lifecycle --> Config_Snapshot_Check
    LoadingCache_Review --> Record_Separately
    Config_Snapshot_Check --> Record_Separately
```

The two branches in the diagram are only the recording order adopted on this page. It does not show the consumer’s internal state machine, nor does it draw `CacheEvent` as a definite connection between the two lines. When the two tasks were previously listed side by side, it was easy to read “both appeared in the same regression round” as “they necessarily followed the same implementation path”; that reading is no longer used.

## Batch Line

The review entry point for batch null caching remains `LoadingCache.java`. First, three observations that might all be referred to as “null caching” must be separated here: the result returned by the batch call contains null; the result container retains null; or the corresponding value can still be seen during a subsequent read. These are not the same thing. The first observation only says something about the result of that call; only after a subsequent read is actually observed is it appropriate to continue discussing cache state.

`HashMap` and `LinkedHashSet` make this entry point worth inspecting first, but they should not be overinterpreted. The former may carry intermediate results, while the latter may retain the key in the request; the actual call site still determines their roles in the batch path. The relationship among loader, key, and value should also be confirmed at the actual references; behavior that does not exist cannot be inferred from a class name or import name.

An earlier record contained a statement that was later retracted:

> A null in the batch read can be understood as the same round of cache invalidation as the anomaly on the notification side.

That statement turned simultaneous observations into causation. The existing materials do not provide the complete relationship from the batch read to notification processing, so retracting it does not mean that another cause has already been found. The decision retained for the batch side is narrower: for each regression, first identify whether the observation lies in the call result, the result set, or the subsequent read; none of these can replace the other two.

This also means that this page does not prescribe a particular null sentinel, container implementation, or loading strategy. None of them has been confirmed by the existing materials. The compatibility window needs records that can be reviewed later, not implementation details that have not been observed written up as standard policy.

## Notification Line

The notification consumer lifecycle must be recorded separately. Here, “lifecycle” cannot be conflated into a single general state: whether a consumer appears, whether it receives a notification, and whether it enters the processing stage are different questions. Without the inputs and outputs in the configuration snapshot, the only statement that can be retained is “the observed results are inconsistent”; no single stage can be arbitrarily selected as the cause.

JCR-223 is the navigation entry point for the notification line. A counterexample was added to this card in 2025-10-21; the counterexample’s specific mechanism is not expanded in the materials on this page, so channels, connections, or processing order are not invented here. The record retained afterward only confirms that one point in the notification-and-broadcast segment remains unconfirmed; the inputs and outputs remain in the configuration snapshot. This counterexample is sufficient to overturn the earlier shared assumption: even if the cache side obtains an explanation first, that does not automatically make the notification side certain.

The notification-side situation also retains one condition: in an environment without old caches or personal configuration, check the creation and non-creation paths. This condition applies only to the notification line. It is not a prerequisite for batch null caching, nor can it be rewritten as an environment requirement that every regression must satisfy. Its purpose is to prevent old caches or personal configuration from entering the judgment of whether a consumer appears.

`CacheEvent` appears in the header of the `LoadingCache` file and can still serve as a hint for continuing to look for event adjacency; it is not evidence that the consumer was created, consumed, or closed. The cache code and notification materials both mention events, which is insufficient to assign the consumer lifecycle to this file.

## Decisions Remaining After Review

JCR-206 moved into review in 2025-09-22, on the grounds at the time that the implementation had been completed in an existing branch; a support scenario was linked the following day. What can be confirmed here is that the change entered review and that a support entry appeared. “Completed in an existing branch” cannot be read as meaning that batch null caching had been verified in every environment.

Therefore, JCR-206 serve on this page as navigation and review context for the batch line, not as approval evidence. The support scenario can help revisit the conditions at the time, but it does not replace the distinction among the batch call, the result set, and the subsequent read. If only one result from the support situation is available, the record should stop at that result and should not be expanded into a conclusion about the entire batch path.

The following decisions are retained for this round:

- Review batch null caching from the batch-read adjacency of `LoadingCache`, recording the call result, result set, and subsequent read separately.
- Check the notification consumer lifecycle against the inputs and outputs in the configuration snapshot, observing the creation or non-creation path under conditions with no old cache and no personal configuration.
- Two observations may be registered in the same regression round, but one observation’s passed, failed, or unconfirmed status cannot be copied to the other.
- `CacheEvent` is retained only as a local event-adjacency hint, not as a conclusion that the notification lifecycle has been implemented or verified.
- JCR-206 and JCR-223 are retained respectively as the review context for the batch line and the navigation entry point for the notification-side situation.

This decision does not isolate the two items as unrelated tasks. They still share the compatibility window of R2026.09, and they may still be discovered together in the same regression. However, when they are cross-referenced, only the shared time window and regression batch should be referenced, not an unconfirmed causal relationship.

The parts not yet filled in should also remain in place: this page has no concrete call sample for batch null caching and no contents of the configuration snapshot. If it is later confirmed that the batch path of `LoadingCache` has a direct reference to event handling, the actual location and the input for that run should be added; if there is no direct relationship, the shared window will remain only release context. The related annotation context parsing and notification process hook are documented separately in DOC-16.

# Annotation Parsing and Notification Interface Proposal

This trial draft retains the early judgment that context parsing and the notification process hook should be on the same path. The issue at the time was not the notification format, but who would pass along to downstream processing what the annotation side already knew. The initial draft treated `CacheManager` as the closer entry point: the file is located at `jetcache-anno/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/anno/support/CacheManager.java`, and within the visible declaration scope it introduced `com.alicp.jetcache.Cache` and `com.alicp.jetcache.anno.CacheConsts`. This is not enough to prove implementation ownership, but it does show that the discussion did not start from the broadcast implementation itself.

The initial proposal was to organize the annotation context as early as possible and then pass it to the notification process hook. That way, the notification side would not need to reinterpret the cache area, cache name, or annotation constants, and a new entry point could reuse the same context. The cost was that the manager side would take on a responsibility that had not previously been confirmed. At the time, “context exists only to serve notifications” was treated as a temporary premise, and other annotation entry points were not laid out one by one.

## Disagreements Left After Review

JCR-207 later described the problem as inconsistent results from annotation context parsing in user environments, and required checking whether paths were created or not created in an environment without old caches or personal configuration. This check changed the focus of the trial: the earlier concern was how the object entered the hook; during review, the more important question was whether the context appeared consistently in a clean environment. A design comparison was recorded on the card, but its result was not written up as a directly adoptable implementation conclusion.

JCR-224 instead checked the notification process hook in a clean working directory, focusing on the exit code, file changes, and residual directories. It cannot be substituted for JCR-207. The former observes the result of the annotation entry point; the latter observes whether an inappropriate working directory remains after processing finishes. The early trial combined the two to reduce the change surface. In retrospect, that arrangement conflates parse failures with unclean processing completion.

The two candidate boundaries are therefore retained without requiring them to be implemented together:

- **Parse early.** `CacheManager` or an adjacent entry point produces the context once, and the notification process hook receives only the result. This is suitable for verifying whether the content is consistent under the same annotation entry point, but it first requires clarification of which fields actually belong to the common context.
- **Fetch on the processing side.** The hook interprets what it needs based on the cache object and annotation information it receives. The change appears local, but it can easily duplicate the parsing rules at another entry point; this option is suitable only for confirming whether the hook already has enough information.
- **Do not connect them yet.** Run the two clean-environment checks separately, record whether the path is created and whether any directory remains, and then decide whether they need to share an object. This choice does not resolve the interface shape; it only avoids using one result to endorse the other.

The earlier statement that “the notification side should not reinterpret annotations” remains here as the approach taken at the time, not as a confirmed constraint. In particular, the existing material does not conclude whether empty expressions, cache-name derivation, and instance identity have already been fixed on the manager side. If these details are valid only at a particular annotation entry point, generating a generic context early would instead broaden the scope of errors.

## Trial Sequence

First reproduce the path examined by JCR-207 in an environment without old caches or personal configuration. Record whether it is created, without mixing cache-hit results from an existing cache into the judgment. Then run the processing corresponding to JCR-224 in a clean working directory, recording the exit code, file changes, and residual directories separately. Once both rounds can complete, compare whether they need the same context; without that comparison, do not add a shared interface.

Two types of failure are acceptable during the process. The first is that the creation path does not produce enough information to make a judgment; in that case, stop discussing the hook parameters and return to the annotation entry point. The second is an abnormal process-hook exit or directory state; in that case, do not attribute the problem to the parsing logic, and do not continue merging just because the context appears complete. Withdraw the respective trial for each type of failure rather than using one change to cover the other.

The condition for withdrawing the “parse early” proposal is that a second set of fields must be added specifically for notifications, or that the same field must be generated by different rules at different annotation entry points. The condition for withdrawing the “fetch on the processing side” proposal is that the hook repeats annotation interpretation to obtain information and that interpretation differs from the one produced by the preceding entry point. After withdrawal, retain `CacheManager` as the place to check back, but do not treat it as the sole owner of the notification logic.

## Not Yet Closed

- What is the minimum content of the context, and does it include annotation information beyond the cache object?
- Can the process hook handle only one call, or does it need to recognize repeated entry for the same cache object?
- When file changes and residual directories occur, are they related to notification processing, or are they left by the execution entry point itself?
- If both checks pass, should the interface have the annotation side provide an object, or only provide an identifier that can be queried again?

This record may still be overturned by the field results from JCR-207 or JCR-224; when citing it, review the check conditions from both cards together rather than taking only the early decision to combine them.

# Jedis Cluster and Channel Decision Record

This page initially placed the Jedis cluster factory and channel opt-in from the R2026.09 compatibility window together because they repeatedly appeared at the same time in the same round of compatibility discussions. The earliest decision, however, was not to combine the two into one implementation task, but to retain separate completion criteria: for the factory, determine whether the inputs can form a sufficient configuration closure; for the channel, determine whether the caller actually has a visible entry point.

The early investigation started with `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/JedisPoolFactory.java`. The package name of this file is `com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure`, and the only type that appears directly at the top is:

```java
import org.springframework.beans.factory.FactoryBean;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import redis.clients.jedis.Jedis;
```

Therefore, the old notes placed it on the starter auto-configuration side rather than first categorizing it as an ordinary cache or broadcast manager. This positioning is still useful: it brings the starting point for reading to the area adjacent to the factory. The statement in the early notes that “verification could be completed from the pool factory” remains a working judgment from that time. The filename, package name, and three direct dependencies are not enough to show which configuration items the cluster inputs pass through, nor are they a substitute for the actual reference relationships.

## Closure approaches compared at the time

There were two approaches at the time. One was to treat the channel as a capability naturally provided by the factory configuration: first clarify the Jedis factory, then mark the channel as available as well. The other was to acknowledge that the two shared a compatibility window while evaluating them separately. The latter was ultimately adopted.

The reason was not that the channel had no connection to the configuration at all, but that the two questions required different missing evidence. The question for the cluster factory was the inputs and configuration closure; the question for channel opt-in was whether the caller could choose to enter the broadcast channel. If the factory’s progress were used to draw a conclusion about the channel, the caller entry point would be obscured by internal configuration checks; conversely, using entry-point discussions to complete the factory’s closure would record an unconfirmed input relationship as already complete.

The old draft stated this decision very briefly: continue looking at the starter on the factory side, and retain a separate entry point on the channel side. When read later, this could easily be misunderstood as meaning two completely unrelated functions. The boundary actually retained is narrower: they can appear in the same compatibility review and can share Jedis’s time window; they simply cannot share one completion signal.

## Follow-up note on the factory track

JCR-211 narrowed the originally broad investigation objective to: check the configuration closure involved in the Jedis cluster factory changes, and return to the corresponding repository file for any missing item. This changed the earlier reading approach. `JedisPoolFactory.java` remains an entry point, but is no longer regarded as the closure itself.

Later records categorized the issue under failure_classified and explicitly noted, “There is still one unconfirmed item in the Jedis cluster factory.” This information invalidated the earlier optimistic closure. It did not specify whether that item was a field, a construction branch, or a runtime result; this page likewise does not fill the gap with seemingly precise implementation details. What can be determined is that the direct dependencies of the factory file alone cannot close this item.

The caller-side issue was later handed to the person responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation. The handoff itself indicates that the subsequent judgment requires an explanation from the compatibility perspective; it does not mean that ownership of the starter implementation has changed, nor that the unconfirmed item has disappeared. If the handoff was read on the old page as meaning “the factory has been confirmed,” this addendum takes precedence: the unconfirmed item remains, and what changed is the entry point for continued verification.

At the time, we also considered recording the missing item uniformly as a Jedis client issue so that it could be grouped with other compatibility matters. This consolidation was not adopted. A gap in the configuration closure must be mapped back to the actual missing repository location; generalizing it as a client issue would instead cause subsequent verification to bypass the original factory path.

## Independent record for the channel track

JCR-228 focuses on the user-visible entry point for channel opt-in. The check it records is to trigger the corresponding job from an existing automation entry point and retain the job, commit, and actual artifact name. This requirement is not intended to add an internal parameter description to the factory; it is intended to let the caller determine whether opt-in appears.

There was a design comparison later. The existing materials preserve neither the complete details of the candidate implementations nor the name or artifact contents of any particular job, so this page does not add a passing result. The only decision retained from that comparison is that channel opt-in continues to be handled as an independent entry point and cannot be subsumed by confirmation of the Jedis cluster factory’s inputs.

There was once a more convenient sequence: look at the factory first, then assume that the channel would appear with the configuration. This sequence was later abandoned. The problem was not that the two had absolutely no technical relationship, but that the object of the check had been replaced by the sequence: the factory track must confirm the configuration closure, while the channel track must confirm the caller entry point and the results left by automation. Establishing the former does not automatically establish the latter.

The interface discussion for the broadcast prefix and Redisson broadcast manager is documented separately in DOC-21. DOC-21 can explain why the broadcast side was compared separately, but should not in turn assign direct responsibility to `JedisPoolFactory.java`, nor can it replace the factory gap left in JCR-211.

## Decisions retained for now

This history does not provide the final input form of the cluster factory, nor does it define the channel’s default behavior. What it retains is a judgment that remains usable but is now tied to its historical context: the cluster factory and channel opt-in are confirmed separately; the starter pool factory file provides navigation to locations adjacent to the factory; and the caller entry point and its automated artifacts are retained under JCR-228.

For the factory track, the old approach of “completing confirmation from one file” no longer applies. When reviewing it, one can still start with the three adjacent points `FactoryBean`, `Autowired`, and `Jedis`, then return to the configuration or reference location based on the missing item. # Broadcast Prefix and Manager Proposal

For R2026.09, we won't treat the broadcast prefix as an incidental parameter of ordinary cache configuration. The trial is to separate out the prefix used for broadcasts and provide an explicit registration point for the Redisson broadcast manager. These two changes are being discussed together because both affect invalidation notifications for multi-level caches; they don't have to share a configuration object, and using the same remote client should not automatically couple them.

There are two candidate approaches.

- Keep using the existing cache-side prefix and have the broadcast manager reuse it directly after reading the configuration. This requires fewer changes, but callers cannot distinguish cache key naming from broadcast channel naming. If a cache region needs a different channel prefix, the configuration semantics become mixed again.
- Define a separate broadcast prefix and read it during manager registration. This adds a configuration entry point, but keeps channel naming within the broadcast boundary. The Redisson adapter would only need to handle that entry point and manager construction, without deriving channels from the ordinary cache name.

The preference is to try the second approach first. Here, “separate” refers only to the configuration and naming boundaries. It does not mean adding a new set of cache key rules, nor should it change the ordinary cache construction path along the way. The Redisson broadcast manager is not a replacement for the existing manager registry either; it is one selectable broadcast implementation in the registry. The registry retains its manager-focused responsibilities, and Redisson adaptation stays at its own integration point, keeping client-specific checks out of cache region configuration.

Use `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/RedisAutoConfiguration.java` as the verification entry point for now. The top of that file shows direct dependencies on `CacheBuilder`, `CacheConfigException`, and `ExternalCacheBuilder`, making it a useful starting point for reading configuration assembly and exception handling. Its location in the starter module only indicates that it is worth checking; whether it actually constructs the Redisson manager still needs to be confirmed by following references.

Check only three outcomes during the trial: specifying a separate broadcast prefix does not overwrite the cache-side prefix; leaving it unspecified does not invent a second naming scheme; and Redisson broadcast registration can coexist with the existing manager registry. If any of these requires ordinary cache configuration to know about Redisson, or requires putting the channel prefix back into the cache name, withdraw the separate entry point, keep the existing prefix path, and handle manager registration separately.

Still undecided: where the default value belongs, and whether missing configuration should prevent startup or fall back to the existing broadcast naming. The former affects how explicit callers must be; the latter affects upgrade costs during the compatibility window. Add repository tests for Redisson broadcast and the current failure output before deciding the default behavior. Until then, do not write up the trial's conclusions as general configuration constraints.

# Jackson Conversion and Broadcast Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally came from a file hit. The search terms included Jackson key conversion, while another incident record mentioned the Spring Data broadcast adapter; the old troubleshooting process casually placed both under the same entry point. During a later review, this order was changed first: the file path is still retained, but attribution must wait until runtime results and object relationships appear; it cannot be filled in from the issue name.

```text
An anomaly is observed
├─ A. Jackson key conversion
│  ├─ Obtain the actual return value
│  │  └─ Record the input, the return value as-is, its type, and where it is used
│  ├─ Obtain an exception
│  │  └─ Record the exception type, the complete message, and the first locatable position
│  └─ Only a search hit or file path is available
│     └─ Stop at the entry point; do not determine the runtime chain
└─ B. Spring Data broadcast adapter
   ├─ Failure while establishing configuration
   │  └─ Save the configuration that triggered it and the original error
   ├─ Failure while sending the broadcast
   │  └─ Save the result of the publishing action
   └─ Failure while receiving or decoding
      └─ Save the received content and the exception boundary
```

## Confirm the evidence in hand first

The first line in on-call records is often only “anomaly after upgrade” or a search result. Both can point to the same file, but they do not support the same judgment. Actual runtime results must be able to answer at least three questions: What object was passed in, what was returned or thrown, and where did the exception occur? If only a path is available, record the path and the object to investigate; do not write the hit count or filename as failure evidence.

The A branch must distinguish between key and value in particular. A result that looks like a conversion failure does not mean that the input was necessarily a key. First paste the input as-is next to the result, preserving quotation marks, null values, and type information. When the return value does not match expectations, write “different result” first; do not directly write that Jackson key conversion has already failed. If `CacheEncodeException` appears in the incident, do not compress the complete exception into “encoding failed”; the exception type and message are the entry point for determining the encoding boundary later. When there is no exception and only a return value, do not replace the observation with an exception name.

The direct dependencies currently visible in the file header are as follows:

```java
import com.alibaba.fastjson.JSON;
import com.alibaba.fastjson.serializer.SerializerFeature;
import com.alicp.jetcache.support.AbstractValueEncoder;
import com.alicp.jetcache.support.CacheEncodeException;
```

These declarations can confirm that there is a local entry point for a Fastjson value encoder here, and can also help trace back the object being encoded and the exception type. They cannot independently confirm the caller of key conversion, much less confirm that a broadcast message passes through this class. If reproduction produces only a value encoding result, retain the result and then find where the actual key was passed in; if it produces only the file header, stop at the file entry point and do not fill in a call relationship.

## A branch: Where the conversion result lands

After obtaining the returned content, first check whether the input and output belong to the same run. Do not reformat the returned content for readability, and do not remove null values. If the conversion result has already been used downstream, also record the usage location and the result separately: the former shows who took the value, while the latter shows what this entry point actually produced. If neither is available, the A branch can only remain in a pending-investigation state.

When an exception is obtained, retain the complete message and the first locatable position. If the exception location is in the value encoder, that only shows that this run failed at the encoding entry point; it does not imply a broadcast-send or receiving-side failure. If the exception location is elsewhere, do not move the exception back just because the investigation search found `FastjsonValueEncoder.java`. Older records placed “the file was hit” before “whether there was a runtime result.” That judgment can still serve as a historical clue, but the troubleshooting order is now reversed.

If the same input produces different results in different environments, first save the original content from both sides side by side. A result changing from a value to an exception and a result changing from a value to empty content require different handling; do not merge them into “environment inconsistency.” The current material does not provide a specific caller, so the call relationship still stops at the position the runtime output can actually point to.

## B branch: Stage assessment for the broadcast adapter

An upgrade-related incident in the Spring Data broadcast adapter must first be assigned to a stage. If it fails while establishing configuration, that means the incident cannot have reached send observation at minimum; if configuration is established successfully but there is no business effect, that does not directly imply that nothing was published; and if content is received but decoding fails, it must not be written as though the sending side did not work.

When the configuration stage fails, save the configuration that actually triggered it and the error; do not change the encoder yet. When the sending stage fails, save the original result corresponding to the publishing action, and record separately whether anything was observed on the receiving side. If content was obtained during the receiving stage but there was no business effect, separate the message content, the receiving result, and the business behavior; when the decoding stage throws an error, retain the received content and exception type, and do not use “did not take effect” in place of the decoding exception.

When all that is known is “regression after upgrade,” retain that scope and do not arbitrarily fill in configuration, sending, receiving, or decoding. If a review also obtains a downloadable artifact, record the artifact and the failure stage separately. The existence of an artifact does not mean that it already contains the fix; when there is no definite object name, do not enter a version number or assume a recovery package.

## File entry point and environment comparison

The currently frozen lookup entry point is:

`samples/simple-samples/src/main/java/FastjsonValueEncoder.java`

The path is recorded in `internal/cache-interop`'s `v_prev`. During the lookup, first inspect the file header and immediate neighbors at the same revision, then place the runtime result back in the corresponding environment. Do not write an entry point found later back into the old path, and do not expand a path comment into implementation ownership.

Record only differences between environments that can be verified on both sides:

- Whether the same input produces the same returned content;
- Whether the return value becomes an exception, empty content, or no result;
- Whether the broadcast failure occurs during configuration, sending, receiving, or decoding;
- Whether the artifacts obtained before and after the upgrade are the same.

If only the environment was changed and the original results from both sides were not saved, this comparison cannot complete the stage assessment. “Normal locally, anomalous in production” can only be recorded as an observed phenomenon; it cannot replace the input, output, and failure location. If a result appears on only one side, first mark the side that is missing; do not assume that the other side performed the same action.

## Boundaries of recovery actions

An older investigation included a record that there was still no output after switching back to the old entry point. This shows that the recovery action produced no observable result, but it cannot by itself establish that the old entry point is incompatible; it is also necessary to confirm whether the input, output, and broadcast stage were actually obtained at the time. Without an execution result, record only “attempted to switch back”; do not write “recovery failed.”

After recovery, the original observation must be repeated. The A branch repeats the same input and saves the result as-is; the B branch repeats the original configuration or publishing action and checks sending, receiving, and decoding separately. If recovery changed only the entry point but not the environment or input, those conditions must still be written next to the result; otherwise the before-and-after results cannot be compared directly.

```text
Result available ──> Compare input and stage ──> Continue investigating object relationships
   │
   └─ No result ──> Retain entry point and gap ──> Do not assign attribution
```

## On-call stop points

1. Only the issue name, call name, or file path is available, with no runtime output: stop at the entry point.
2. `FastjsonValueEncoder.java` was seen, but it has not been confirmed whether the input is a key or a value: stop at object confirmation.
3. The broadcast has no business effect, but it has not been confirmed whether sending occurred: stop at the sending boundary.
4. There is only a post-upgrade failure, with no failure stage: retain “regression after upgrade” and do not specify a recovery target.
5. The exception message was truncated: obtain the original exception again and do not replace it with a summary sentence.

What this page can currently confirm is the file entry point, the local dependencies, and that the two symptoms should be handled separately. The actual caller of Jackson key conversion, whether the Spring Data broadcast adapter is connected to this value encoder, and exactly which stage the broadcast stops at must all wait until the corresponding runtime records appear before the assessment is updated.

1. First confirm that the call name corresponding to the old path and the factory compatibility check are still the same matter.
2. Inspect the builder declaration and its reference adjacency in `v_prev`, and record the object relationship that can actually be seen.

This page does not list the names of specific compatible callers, nor does it retain the release command from any particular migration. Migration batches can therefore be supplemented only according to the actual verification results; the call chain must not be inferred from words such as factory and builder. The earliest record contained only a path and a guess about where the implementation lived:

> The old investigation can be traced back to `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/ConfigTree.java` using the issue name and call name. Since the filename appears alongside the ConfigTree string properties, the handling is probably here.

```java
package com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure;
import org.springframework.core.env.ConfigurableEnvironment;
import org.springframework.core.env.EnumerablePropertySource;
import org.springframework.core.env.PropertySource;
```

These declarations point the search toward Spring environment properties. They do not establish the full relationship: which object the string properties pass through, where they are retrieved, or who receives them afterward. On later review, we separated “we can locate the file” from “this file is ultimately responsible.”

## Initial decision

There were three ways to handle this at the time:

| Option | What to retain | Direct cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Record `ConfigTree.java` as the entry point to the complete implementation | Easy to retrace, but assigns responsibility prematurely |
| B | Put the page on hold until a complete reproduction is available | A firmer conclusion, but an existing starting point would be temporarily unavailable |
| C | Keep the file as a starting point and list unconfirmed relationships separately | Readers need to distinguish the path from the findings |

We chose C. The old investigation had already provided a stable path, so there was no need to remove it entirely. But we had neither an observed call nor output after property retrieval, so we could not include A’s stronger claim in this decision. The page continues to use “ConfigTree string properties” as its subject, meaning that this is what we are investigating—not that this file has been established as containing its entire implementation.

The three types in the file header are therefore recorded only as direct dependencies. `ConfigurableEnvironment` is a lead for the environment object; `EnumerablePropertySource` and `PropertySource` are leads for property source types. At this stage, we are not treating imports as method calls or rewriting a list of types as an execution sequence.

## Where the autumn review stopped

The review of JCR-216 was first marked blocked on 2025-10-06, with the reason that the read-only account needed for reproduction was still awaiting approval. Later that day, it returned to the backlog because production issues took priority that cycle and this would be scheduled next cycle. This period produced no return values, exception output, or caller names that could be added to the page.

We can now write “start investigating from this file,” but not “string property handling is completed here.”

1. Whether `ConfigTree.java` contains local declarations or relationships that correspond to string property retrieval.
2. Whether the retrieved values pass through users’ normal calls and can yield a return value or raw diagnostics that can be retained.

The first item is a check of relationships within the file; the second requires observing the actual usage path. Seeing an intermediate state only at a debug entry point is not enough to answer the second question. There are no results available to cite, so both items remain unconfirmed.

DOC-26 is review material for an adjacent interface in the same compatibility window; this page does not use it to fill in implementation details for ConfigTree.

| Treat the filename as the conclusion | Immediately provide an implementation location | Conflate the entry point with the consumption point |
| Write nothing for now | Wait for the complete relationship and a reproduction to appear | The old investigation could no longer be used |
| Record the entry point and the gap | Preserve partial file material and open questions to verify | The page would not give an overly early final ownership assignment |

Adopt the third option. Not because the information was already complete, but because the material available at the time was only sufficient to support a limited decision. The page can state clearly where the file is, what types appear in the file header, and how old records point here; it cannot also claim which object receives the string value, or that this value has already been returned by a user call.

This choice also affects “history” in the title. What is recorded here is how the judgment narrowed from “it looks like it is in ConfigTree” to “start by checking ConfigTree,” rather than presenting an object relationship that is not yet fully established as a formal definition. The strong assertion on the old page is retained to explain why the wording had to change later; it no longer stands alongside the current position as one of two equally valid conclusions.

## Local facts from the file header

The declarations left in the `ConfigTree.java` file header are:

```java
package com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure;

import org.springframework.core.env.ConfigurableEnvironment;
import org.springframework.core.env.EnumerablePropertySource;
import org.springframework.core.env.PropertySource;
```

The package declaration places the file in the `com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure` namespace. It can help readers confirm the file’s relationship to the group of names associated with starter auto-configuration, but the package name itself does not answer which object ultimately uses the string property.

`ConfigurableEnvironment`, `EnumerablePropertySource`, and `PropertySource` are direct dependencies visible in the file header. They provide three type clues to look at first when examining the code: the environment object, enumerable property sources, and general property sources. The available material preserves neither snippets of calls to these types within a method nor the result returned after obtaining the value, so the page keeps them next to the file entry point rather than arranging the three into an execution chain.

“Direct dependencies” here is a file-header-level description. It is not another name for runtime relationships. For example, seeing `ConfigurableEnvironment` allows further investigation into where environment properties are read; seeing `PropertySource` allows further checking of how property sources are accessed; but these two names alone cannot justify naming a caller that does not appear in the file. This limitation is not a separate explanation, but the reason this page stops its record at the file header.

| Material available at the time | Judgment that can currently be retained | Object questions still unresolved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File path | Start tracing back from `ConfigTree.java` | Whether it is the final consumption point |
| `package` declaration | The file belongs to `com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure` | Whether the package name corresponds to a runtime owner |
| Three imports | The file header contains type clues for the environment and property sources | Which method actually obtains the string |
| Pointers from the old investigation | The issue name and call name can lead readers back to this path | Whether the old pointers already cover the complete call relationships |

This table only separates four kinds of evidence; it does not turn gaps into new conclusions. It also explains why the early pages can continue to be referenced: the entry information has not become invalid; what became invalid was the step of directly equating the entry with ownership.

## An Incomplete Review

JCR-216 in the historical actions of 2025-10-06 first moved the reproduction task from To Do to Blocked. The specific reason recorded was that the read-only account needed for reproduction was still pending approval. At around 15:20 that day, the work was moved from Blocked back to To Do because online issues would be handled first this cycle and scheduled for the next cycle.

This history contains no reproduction result. It cannot be polished into “verified failure,” nor can it be written as saying that a configuration value was empty, erroneous, or successful. The only confirmed fact is that the reproduction conditions were not ready during that handling window, after which the work was returned to the backlog.

A public comment on the card from the same day contains another correction: in the Starter configuration section, one point concerning the ConfigTree string property remained unconfirmed. Here, the “correction” addresses the page’s tendency to state the file location too definitively. It did not provide the object name, caller name, or return value for that point, so the page continues to leave it unconfirmed rather than supplying a name.

The earlier TODO can therefore be separated into four distinct gaps:

- Whether a local declaration directly corresponding to the action of obtaining the string property exists inside the file;
- Whether `ConfigurableEnvironment`, `EnumerablePropertySource`, and `PropertySource` all actually participate in that action;
- Which routine user call passes through this relationship;
- Whether that call can leave a return value or raw diagnostic.

These four items do not share a single answer source. The first and second require returning to the local code in the file; the third requires finding the usage path; the fourth requires a review artifact that can be retained. Compressing them into “pending confirmation” would prevent readers from seeing which layer to investigate next, so they are left separate for now.

## A Change in the Review Method

The local description for JCR-216 requires the “ConfigTree string property” to be exercised through a routine user call rather than a debugging entry point, with the return value or raw diagnostic retained. This requirement specifically changes the verification procedure, but it does not automatically turn `ConfigTree.java` into the final consumption point.

The current review is understood as two consecutive steps: first, start from the file entry point to check the local declarations and relationships concerning the sources of properties; then, put the same object back into the user's everyday calls and observe what results can be retained. The first step answers “what relationships exist in the file,” and the second answers “what path is taken during use.” The debugging entry point can, at most, provide intermediate observations; it cannot replace the everyday calls in the second step.

“Retaining return values or raw diagnostics” also has a clearly defined scope here: the return values actually observed must be retained, or unprocessed diagnostic material must be retained. The current page has no such samples, so “should be retained” is not written as “has been retained.” Nor is there any material showing that approval for the read-only account was subsequently completed, so the blocker that autumn cannot be retroactively rewritten as a successful reproduction.

If review results become available in the future, they should align with the local relationships in the file. A new issue name alone, the same old link, or another occurrence of this path still only shows that the lookup entry point has not changed; it cannot automatically close out the object relationships. This distinction is the practical purpose of retaining the autumn record in the current version: it explains why the page still has empty items, rather than manufacturing a failure case.

## Options Compared and the Decision

**Option One: File location determines implementation ownership.**

This is closest to the early intuition. Readers can get a short answer just by seeing `ConfigTree.java`, and maintenance costs are low. But it treats the navigation results from the earlier investigation as call relationships, and import names as read operations that have already occurred. If it is later discovered that the string properties are retrieved by another object, the page would have to be retracted in its entirety, so this option was not adopted.

**Option Two: Save the page only after all relationships are confirmed.**

This approach avoids premature conclusions, but would lose the paths, package names, and file-header dependencies that are already valuable. People returning to the earlier investigation still need a location that leads back to the source file; waiting for everything also cannot explain the misreading at the time. A complete pause was not adopted.

**Option Three: Record only the card, not the source file.**

The card can specify the requirements for everyday calls and result retention, but it cannot replace the file path. Saving only the card would tell readers how to review, but not where to start reading. This option was not adopted either.

**Option Four: Retain the entry point and separate ownership from results.**

This is the current decision. The file path, package declaration, and three direct dependencies are retained as entry-point material; the object that retrieves the string properties, the consuming code, and the return values are retained as items awaiting verification; everyday calls and raw diagnostics are retained as review conditions. This option does not provide the shortest one-sentence conclusion, but it matches the granularity of the existing material.

Choosing Option Four also brings a practical compatibility cost: readers need to look at both the file layer and the call layer, rather than judge solely by the filename. This cost is acceptable, because the more convenient alternative would entrench unconfirmed relationships in the knowledge base. When new results are added in the future, object relationships or diagnostics only need to be added at the corresponding gaps; the existing entry point and early judgments do not need to be deleted.

## Decision Details

The current position is fixed as follows:

- `jetcache-starter/jetcache-autoconfigure/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/autoconfigure/ConfigTree.java` remains the verification entry point for ConfigTree string properties.
- The `package com.alicp.jetcache.autoconfigure;` in the file header remains as file location information.
- `ConfigurableEnvironment`, `EnumerablePropertySource`, and `PropertySource` remain as direct dependencies and lookup clues.
- The existing navigation relationship from the issue name and call name to this path remains valid.
- The path, package declaration, and import do not independently constitute complete implementation ownership.
- Without a return value or raw diagnostic sample, do not register a runtime result.
- Verification should prioritize going through the user’s routine call, rather than observing only the debug entry.

What is being decided here is how the document records existing decisions and the order of the next verification steps, not whether to modify the code implementation. The existing materials provide no basis for concluding that changing `ConfigTree.java` would complete the compatibility window, nor do they identify another owner that can be named directly. Therefore, the current page stores the file entry and the ownership determination separately.

## Path diagram

The state diagram below retains only the verification nodes that have already appeared on this page; it does not indicate the execution order among the three import statements:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> File entry
    File entry --> Local declaration
    Local declaration --> User routine call
    User routine call --> Return value or raw diagnostic
    Local declaration --> Unconfirmed relationship
    Return value or raw diagnostic --> [*]
```

“Unconfirmed relationship” in the diagram corresponds to the object relationship that is still missing. It is not an already named code object. “Return value or raw diagnostic” in the diagram corresponds to the verification artifacts that JCR-216 require to be retained; it has not been marked as already existing. The purpose of the state diagram is to separate the entry, in-file checking, routine use, and result retention; it cannot be treated as evidence of a call chain.

## Order of use for the verification entry

When you receive an old issue name or call name, first return to `internal/cache-interop`’s `ConfigTree.java` and confirm the package declaration and direct dependencies in the file header. Do not jump directly from the filename to implementation ownership. Then inspect the action that obtains the string property within the local scope of the same file; if the local material still cannot establish the object relationship, retain “unconfirmed relationship” and do not substitute the module name for the object name.

Once the local relationship has a result, check whether it is reached through a user’s routine call. A routine call here is not an alias for the debug entry; it must explain how the call reaches that object. If a value is observed, retain the return value; if no value is present but a raw diagnostic is produced, retain the original diagnostic. If neither is available, the page can only record that verification produced no output; it should not turn the blank into success or failure.

No specific name is provided for the routine invocation entry, nor are there a return value, original diagnostic, or caller code snippet. This gap must remain in the document, because adding a seemingly reasonable name would change the factual scope of the event record. Read-only account approval and the priority of online work explain why the previous round stopped, but they are not a guarantee of subsequent results.

## Why the Earlier Judgment Was Not Deleted

The earlier statement that “processing should be in the ConfigTree section” is no longer the current conclusion, but it still has historical value. It shows where the misunderstanding originated: the search terms simultaneously matched starter, configtree, environment, and value, and the file header did in fact contain Spring property-source types, so the file location looked like the answer to where it belonged.

If this statement were simply deleted, later readers would see only the narrowed position and would not know why it was necessary to distinguish the entry point from the consumption point. Keeping the original text and correcting it afterward shows what counterexample triggered the change in understanding: the file path and type declarations did not provide a caller, return value, or original diagnostic. This is not using hindsight to correct the earlier author; it is putting the earlier judgment back in its original context, when the available information was insufficient.

Likewise, the blocking record from the autumn is not rewritten as “review failed.” The reason for the block was read-only account approval, and the reason for returning to the to-do list was to address online issues first; neither describes the runtime result of the ConfigTree string property. The current decision uses them only to explain why the review was not completed, and does not infer a technical conclusion from the state transitions.

## Items That Are Still Open

1. The local location of the corresponding string-property retrieval operation in `ConfigTree.java`.
2. The actual relationship at that location between `ConfigurableEnvironment` and the two property-source types.
3. The specific entry point and caller object used by the user's routine invocation.
4. A verifiable return value or original diagnostic.
5. Once the read-only account condition is available, whether the review can answer the first four items.

These items cannot substitute for one another. Finding the file location completes only the first layer of navigation; confirming an import does not automatically provide a return value; obtaining one observation from a debug entry point still does not fulfill the routine invocation requirement. When adding material next time, place it under the corresponding item and retain this page's path and earlier judgment.

## Adjacent Material

JCR-216 is the only card on this page that requires direct navigation. It narrows the review from “look at some debug location” to the user's routine invocation and requires retaining the return value or original diagnostic. The card does not provide a caller name or result, so it serves only this local requirement.

DOC-26 are adjacent API reviews within the same compatibility window. Their subject is Lettuce topology refresh, not the ConfigTree string property. The two pages can serve as navigation to each other within the same window, but the API determination from DOC-26 must not be moved into this page, nor should this page's file header be used to explain the connection relationship on that page.

## Current stopping point

The decision ultimately retained on this page is: continue using `ConfigTree.java` as the verification entry point, withdraw the strong claim that the file location represents complete ownership; use the package declaration in the file header and the three direct dependency descriptions to describe the local context; use users' routine calls, return values, or original diagnostics to define the visible artifacts for the next review; and explicitly leave blank fields when there is no supporting material for the object relationships and results.

This is sufficient to support continued follow-up on the previous investigation without disguising a path as a complete implementation description. If an actual call relationship is found later, that relationship and its corresponding result should be added; if the same path or issue name is obtained again, the current decision on this page remains unchanged.

# Lettuce Topology Refresh Proposal

The earliest records attributed only the issue in the R2026.09 compatibility window to Lettuce topology refresh; only later was the actual investigation scope narrowed to one file. We still start from `jetcache-support/jetcache-redis-lettuce/src/main/java/com/alicp/jetcache/redis/lettuce/RedisLettuceCache.java`, but this is merely the existing investigation entry point and is insufficient to attribute the creation, trigger, or result of the refresh to that file.

The contents that can be verified from the file header are as follows:

```java
package com.alicp.jetcache.redis.lettuce;
import com.alicp.jetcache.*;
import com.alicp.jetcache.external.AbstractExternalCache;
import com.alicp.jetcache.support.JetCacheExecutor;
```

These declarations indicate that it is adjacent to the Lettuce cache implementation. `AbstractExternalCache` and `JetCacheExecutor` are direct dependencies. They do not justify inferring nonexistent method names, nor treating connection initialization, connection reuse, and topology refresh as the same action. The old draft described the file location more like a responsibility location. That judgment should remain in the history, but this version no longer uses it as a premise for the proposal.

## Candidates to Retain

Candidate one is to trigger the refresh near the existing Lettuce connection-reuse entry point. It is closer to the site of the legacy-call failure and has a narrower trial scope. The drawback is that a legacy call may reuse a connection first and then trigger a topology update; if the endpoint leaves only a final state, it is impossible to tell whether the failure occurred during connection reuse or refresh. This candidate cannot be considered the trigger point merely because it is adjacent in the path.

Candidate two is to trigger it adjacent to connection initialization or configuration application. This places the action at a clearer initialization boundary, making it easier to compare behavior before and after initialization. The cost is that every instance passing through the entry point may be affected, while ordinary cache users may not need this refresh. If the issue occurs only in legacy calls, expanding the initialization scope would also turn the compatibility window into a connection behavior change. The current material does not prove that this entry point exists, so it remains only a candidate.

There is also a variant that does not change the trigger location: continue tracing through the file declarations and adjacent Lettuce objects, confirm which object the legacy call actually passes through, and then decide where to trial it. This variant does not directly resolve the failure, but it avoids mistaking the file path for the call relationship. If the trace still does not identify the actual trigger point, do not casually expand the scope to the manager registry, annotation context, or other cache backends.

## Verification Actions

The entry description later left by JCR-217 is: run “Lettuce topology refresh” through the user's usual entry point, and save the terminal output and workspace side effects separately. It provides a verification action, not a conclusion that an implementation location has been determined. The current material also does not include the complete output from that run, so this document cannot describe the refresh as a single verified success or failure.

Keep the two kinds of records distinct. The terminal may show a call failure while the workspace shows no change within the same scope; or the call may not report an immediate error while the connection state has already changed. The former does not directly prove that the workspace operation failed, and the latter does not establish that the topology was refreshed based solely on the absence of an error. Trial records must retain, at minimum, the entry point, the verbatim terminal output, and the workspace side effects as observed in each case. They must not be replaced with a single statement that “the refresh succeeded.”

This version does not adopt the approach of “change only one configuration value and check the result.” Changing a configuration value alone may make the result look like refresh took effect when it actually only re-established the connection; directly replacing the entire Lettuce initialization path would introduce more connection behavior. The smaller trial should hold the user entry point and existing cluster shape constant, and observe only whether a refresh action occurs, what the terminal outputs, and what workspace side effects appear. “Constant” here describes a comparison condition, not a commitment already made about the current implementation.

## Unresolved After Review

The old draft leaned toward triggering the refresh adjacent to connection reuse because it was close to the problem site. After review, that reason supports only candidate one, not a final decision. If the actual trigger point is in an adjacent object, the proposal should move accordingly; if the action can be observed only at the initialization boundary, the impact scope must be recalculated. We cannot continue to strongly attribute the issue to `RedisLettuceCache` merely because the issue name and call name once pointed here.

The handling of failure output is also undecided. Trial code should not rewrite an exception as success, and it should not issue a compatibility conclusion without a corresponding workspace record. The exception type, the specific change to cluster URI, and the compatibility differences among the different Lettuce entry points are all unresolved in the existing records; this version must not turn them into interface constraints.

## Rollback Boundary

If the added refresh handling causes connection initialization to fail, or if the ordinary cache path exhibits behavior that was not present before, first remove the added entry point and restore the original connection path. If the terminal output cannot be correlated with the workspace side effects, stop expanding the trial as well; do not treat retry results as a determination of the cause. After rollback, retain the failure output and the file location that has already been rechecked. These materials can support the next investigation, but they cannot establish that the original cause of the failure has been determined.

This version can therefore support a local comparison of candidates, but it cannot serve as the current authoritative implementation description for Lettuce topology refresh. The next actual verification must first fill in the object relationship through which the legacy call passes, and then choose between the two placement points. Until then, the initialization location, reuse location, and specific exception remain undecided.

At the time, jetcache test · Quality Signal Desk did not rebuild the environment first. Keeping it first was the only way to distinguish whether later differences came from the environment, the command, or the recording method; if the environment was rebuilt first and the original state changed, the comparison could only be reconstructed from memory and screenshots.

There were two options on the table. The decision was to retain the `current revision` first and not rebuild the environment for this trade-off; at the recording layer, list `multi-level` separately and temporarily do not merge it back into `cache name`. # Troubleshooting Tree for Stalled Runtime Observability

When runtime observability stops progressing from the “current entry point,” branch based on the objects visible in the live state. Follow only one branch at a time; if there is no evidence for the preceding step, stop there rather than treating a guess as the root cause.

## Entry branches

- If you can still find `annotation context` on the page or in the output, first note its corresponding `source id`, then follow that object back to review `jetcache-core-operations-observability`. Do not clean up the live state or retry first.
- If you only have `cache area` and no `annotation context`, preserve the raw content and check whether it can still be matched to the current entry point. If it cannot, stop and hand off to the permissions owner; do not infer object relationships from names.
- If the entry point displays `Lettuce connection`, first record it as a connection-related clue alongside the live state, not as grounds for concluding that there is a connection failure. A new trace or version information is needed to continue.

## When evidence is available

1. You can see `source id`, but there is no subsequent topology information: stop at this node and preserve the first failing sample, run id, trace, and version.
2. You have seen `topology refresh`: confirm whether it occurred after this entry-point action. If there is no event ordering or trace, stop here as well; do not substitute a historical successful sample for this observation.
3. You have `ordered key`, but `monitor lifecycle` has not advanced to the next step: record the `cache area` containing the key and the location of the first anomaly, then hand off through the Runtime Observability project's maintenance entry point. Do not keep guessing about the caller here.
4. You only have a permissions error, restricted details, or unreadable attachments: record the visible error and entry-point address, then hand off directly to the permissions owner. Do not perform recovery actions until the permissions issue is resolved.

## Stopping and handing off

Stop if any of the following occurs: the first failing sample has been overwritten; the current entry point can no longer be matched to `source id`; the ordering of `topology refresh` is unclear; there are only screenshots and no trace to review; or runtime observability is now showing a permissions error. Include the raw sample, run id, trace, version, and the branch reached in the handoff. Do not state an unverified final cause.

Earlier records show that retrying too soon made it difficult to compare the original failing sample and environment differences. Preserve the first failure before deciding whether to retry. Recovery actions have not yet been validated in the shared environment; if the behavior after a retry differs, save both results separately without overwriting the original record.

This page only covers branches after entering runtime observability from the current entry point. Do not fold input replay in adjacent projects, caller integration testing, or other cache issues into the same tree.

# Compatibility Directory Entry Migration Index

The migration log starts with `docs/adj-jetcache-anno/migration/Current Entry-Legacy Entry Migration Index.md`. Similarly named side paths are not folded in here; each item corresponds only to a legacy entry retained in the compatibility directory, its replacement location, and the callers still using that entry.

The directory covers public contracts formed around schema and api. A legacy entry is not deleted merely because a new location has appeared in the directory: callersFang Ke can still read records from the old location, or only part of the compatibility adjustments may have been completed. Migration is considered complete based on confirmation from actual users, not on whether the new entry has appeared in the directory.

## Index Entry Requirements

Keep one separate record for each legacy entry, documenting at least:

| Record item | Content to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Legacy entry | Original name and current status; entries that can no longer be traced back remain marked as expired |
| Replacement location | The location to switch to and whether it carries compatibility content for schema or api |
| Callers | Callers still using the legacy entry; if no caller has been confirmed, do not mark the item complete |
| Migration status | Not started, migration in progress, confirmed, or legacy entry restored |
| Exit criteria | The item's own completion criteria and maintenance arrangements |

Legacy records may remain in the directory. Their purpose is to tell callers where they used to enter, not to treat expired content as the current contract again. Do not fill in speculation for notes that cannot be traced back, and do not change their status to migrated merely because a replacement location exists.

## Migration Order

Start with one legacy entry, verify its associated schema or api contract, and then check which callers still use it. Once it is confirmed that the callers can switch to the replacement location, update that record's status; if callers in the same group use different entries, record them separately rather than replacing item-by-item confirmation with a directory-level summary.

The replacement location takes on only compatibility content that has been confirmed. If callers need to retain the legacy entry, keep the record as “Migration in progress” and note that the legacy entry is still being used. The new location in the directory and the callers' actual switch are two separate things; the former cannot serve as a conclusion about the latter.

Each item has its own schedule, owner, and exit criteria. The index records migration relationships only; a single record must not promise a shared completion time for adjacent items. Callers that have not yet been confirmed remain under the original entry until usage results are available to update the status.

## Return to the Legacy Entry

When the replacement location can no longer meet a caller's needs, first restore that caller to the corresponding legacy entry, then change the index status to “Legacy entry restored.” Do not delete the replacement location or erase the migration record; retaining it shows which compatibility relationship the restoration occurred in. After restoration, recheck the public schema and api contracts to avoid recording one caller's rollback as abandonment of migration for the entire directory.

Restoring a legacy entry affects only callers confirmed to need restoration. Other entries with confirmed migrations retain their respective statuses until their own exit criteria are met.
